text: Given a string s, return true if s can be a palindrome after deleting at most one character.

Thanks. Before I dive in, I'd like to clarify a few things. At most one includes deleting zero, so a string that's already a palindrome returns true? And it's lowercase letters only, and I delete at most one index?
Okay. So my starting idea: converge with two pointers from both ends, and on the first mismatch, spend the one deletion on one of the two conflicting characters.

Let me reason about where the deletion goes. A naive approach would delete each index and re-check the rest. That's n checks of linear time each, so quadratic. This problem reminds me of converging two pointers: a palindrome is just mirror pairs matching from the ends inward. When I hit s of l not equal to s of r, everything outside l and r already matches, so the deletion must be s of l or s of r. Deleting anywhere else can't fix this pair. So I check l plus one through r, or l through r minus one. That fork happens only once, so it stays linear time.

Here's the plan. One: move l and r inward while the characters match. Two: on the first mismatch, return whether skipping the left or skipping the right leaves a plain palindrome. Three: if the pointers meet with no mismatch, return true. Two things worth flagging. The helper is zero-tolerance. If it also allowed a delete, that would be two deletions total. And I pass the string by reference with indices, not substrings, to keep constant extra space. Does this approach sound good, or would you rather I think of another way?

Let me write it. A private helper, is palindrome, runs a plain two-pointer check on l through r with no tolerance. The main function converges from both ends, and on the first mismatch it returns the helper on l plus one through r, or the helper on l through r minus one. One detail worth flagging: the or short-circuits. If deleting the left works, it never tries the right, so the fork is at most two passes. And the return sits right at the fork, so it can only happen once.

Let's dry-run c b b c c, the case where only one side works. The outer c's match. Then at positions one and three, b against c is the mismatch, so we fork. Deleting the left leaves b c, not a palindrome. Deleting the right leaves b b, a palindrome, so true. Delete-left fails but delete-right succeeds, which is why both are needed. Corner cases: a b c is false, since both forks fail. A b a is true, and it never forks. A single character is true.

Time is linear. The main converge is one pass, and the fork triggers at most two more linear checks, once. Space is constant extra: just indices, and the helper takes the string by reference, so no substrings. One more thing: at most one is what keeps it linear. With k deletions, each mismatch could fork again, so it becomes a memoized search over l, r, and deletions left. And a replace-instead-of-delete variant is even simpler: just count mismatched pairs.

Nicely done. Three things stood out: arguing the delete must be one of the two conflicting characters, the zero-tolerance helper so it's at most one deletion, and passing by reference to stay at constant extra space. Good work.
